title: Out-of-stock states that keep the sale later
metaTitle: Out-of-stock states that keep the sale
excerpt: Say the item is gone, offer a way to hear when it returns, and do not leave a live add-to-cart button. A dead control with no sentence feels like a broken shop.
alt: A wide city avenue with yellow taxis, tall buildings, and people on the sidewalk. The street keeps moving, and the shop still has to say when an item is gone.
caption: A busy avenue, and a status the shop still owes. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an out-of-stock product page say?
faqs.answer: Say which item is gone, in the same place as the price and the action. If only one size or color is unavailable, say that, and leave the others purchasable. If the product will not return, say so, and do not offer a waitlist that will never send.

faqs.question: Should the add-to-cart button stay on an out-of-stock page?
faqs.answer: No. A button labeled add to cart still describes a purchase, even when it is gray and disabled. Replace it with a different action, such as a request to be emailed when that variant returns, or remove it and leave a sentence. A control that does nothing when tapped feels like the shop is down.

faqs.question: What belongs in a back-in-stock email?
faqs.answer: Name the product, the variant, and the current price, and link to the page where it can be bought. Say if it may sell out again. Send the note only when the buy path works. If you will not restock, tell the people who asked, once, instead of leaving them in silence.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Out of stock UX is a status, a next step, and a control that tells the truth. Say the item is gone, offer a way to hear when it returns, and do not leave an add-to-cart button that still looks alive. A gray button with no sentence feels broken, and a broken page does not save the next sale.

People judge a page in the opening seconds. Nielsen Norman Group’s article on [how long users stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/), written by Jakob Nielsen in 2011, reports that people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that a clear value proposition in the first 10 seconds is what earns more of their time. On a product page the value is the object and whether they can have it. If that fact is late, the photography does not get a chance.

## Say it is gone where they expected to buy

Put the status beside the price, in the same block as the action. Use the shop’s ordinary voice. “Sold out” or “Out of stock” is enough when the whole product is gone. When the page has sizes or colors, name the one that is gone. “Navy in medium is gone. The other sizes are in stock.” A sitewide banner that says some items are unavailable does not help the person looking at this object.

Write the status as text. Color alone will not carry it. The [W3C’s WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) groups the guidelines under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A status that exists only as a gray fill is easy to miss, including for someone who does not see that gray the way you do. Hanabi does not certify a shop against WCAG. The principle still decides where the sentence sits: in the content, next to the control, available to a person and to software that does not interpret your color.

Match the state to the object on screen. If one variant is gone, do not mark the whole product gone. If the whole product is gone, do not leave a size picker that implies a choice. When the shopper changes size, the status should change with it, without a reload that loses their place on the page.

Keep the URL. A campaign, an old email, or a saved link should land on this product, not on a soft error that looks like a missing template. The title of the page can carry the product name and the fact that it is currently unavailable, so a search result does not promise a purchase the page will refuse.

## The control should look finished

Remove the purchase action, or replace it with a control that does a different job. A button that still says “Add to cart,” even disabled, describes a purchase. People tap it. On a phone, that tap is the test. If nothing happens, they assume the shop is down, and they leave with that impression of the brand.

“Email me when it returns” is a different action, and it should look like that action. If you keep a disabled control so the layout does not jump, put a visible sentence beside it, and do not make that control the only thing in the block. The understandable principle in WCAG is the practical test. A person can tell what is unavailable, and they can reach the alternative without guessing which gray shape still works.

Leave the price visible unless you truly do not know the restock price. A missing price plus a dead button reads as an unfinished template. The price says the object is real and the shop knows what it costs. If the price may change when the item returns, say that in the request copy. Do not blank the page to avoid the question.

Do not put a scarcity line on an item that is already gone. “Only a few left” on an empty shelf is a second falsehood. The first was a live-looking purchase control. Scarcity belongs on an item someone can still buy, and only when it is true.

## A way to hear when it returns

The way back is a short form, not a new account. Email is enough for most brand shops. Ask for the address, name the variant they were viewing, and say what you will send. “We will email you once, when the navy medium is available to buy.” One message. A specific object. A newsletter checkbox can exist only as its own control, unchecked, with its own sentence. Do not fold the list signup into the restock request.

Confirm on the page, in text. “You will hear if this returns.” That is the receipt. If the address is invalid, name the field and how to fix it. A red border with no sentence leaves them unsure whether the request exists. The same standard you would use on a checkout error belongs here, because this form is the only path left.

Store the request against the variant, not only the parent product. A note that “the jacket is back,” when only one size returned, trains people to ignore the sender. When you do send the note, link to that variant. Say if the price moved. Send it when the item can actually be bought. A message that arrives while the purchase control is still dead is another broken promise.

If you cannot run the list, do not offer the form. A clear sentence, plus a path to what is in stock, is more honest than a waitlist nobody watches. Someone has to own failed sends, bounced mail, and the day the item comes back. That owner is an operations fact, not a plugin setting you discover in the complaints.

## What stays on the page

Keep the photographs, the materials, and the short description. The person may still be deciding whether to wait. They need the facts they would have used to buy. Shipping and returns can remain as quiet lines if they will be true for a later order. Do not route those lines into a checkout they cannot enter.

Show objects that are actually available, with names and prices. “Other colors in stock” helps when those colors are the same product. A generic “you may also like” row is a different module, and it should not cover the status. The news comes first. Alternatives come after the person has understood it.

If the object is discontinued, say that in the same block. “We are not making this again” is kinder than a form that will never fire. Point at a current object only when it is honestly close, and label it as a different product. A similar photograph with no explanation feels like a redirect.

Down the Cove, a public Hanabi ecommerce migration and redesign, is the kind of shop where this screen has to be designed with the product page, not patched on after launch. The empty size is a state in the system. It has copy, a control, and a next step. A theme default is not that state.

## Recommendations that do not bury the news

A grid under the fold can help a shopper who is willing to switch. It hurts when it replaces the sentence. Open the page on a phone and read the first screen aloud. You should be able to say whether you can buy the object, what it costs, and what to do if you cannot. If the first screen is only a carousel of other goods, the page is avoiding the news.

Label the row as other products. Each tile needs a name, a price, and a real link. A tile with no price sends them into a second surprise. If that product is also unavailable, do not offer it as the rescue.

When the item returns, the same URL should show a working purchase path. People who were not on the list still need to buy. The email is a message. The page is the shop. Do not leave the waitlist form in the hero after the object is available again. Move it off, or show it only on variants that are still gone.

Campaign pages and ads should learn the same status. Sending paid traffic to a product you know is gone, with no status designed, spends the click to teach people the shop feels broken. If the campaign must stay up, the landing state is this one: a true sentence, a way to be told, and no fake purchase.

## The note you send later

Write the return message as a person in the shop would write it. Name the product, the variant, and the price. Link to the page. Say the item can sell out again if that is true. Do not attach a discount unless you meant to run one. A surprise code teaches people to wait for a code next time, which fights the reason you wrote to them.

If you will not restock, send that once to the people who asked. Silence after a promise is how a list becomes a complaint thread. One plain sentence is enough. “We are not bringing this size back. Here is what is in the line now,” with a link, closes the loop.

Match the voice of the shop. A heritage craft brand and a calm lifestyle brand should not share a bulk template with three exclamation marks. Thomas Bewick’s public site is an editorial heritage project, and Wabisabi’s is a calm brand site. A restock note for either should sound like the pages those customers already read. The sentence can be short. It has to be specific.

If several variants return on the same day, one message can list them. A burst of separate emails will be filtered, and then the restock that mattered never gets seen. Keep each line tied to a variant someone asked for. Do not use the list to announce unrelated products.

## Check the state before you call it done

Walk the page as a shopper who arrived from a link to that exact object.

1. Read the first screen and say whether you can buy it.
2. Try the control. It should not describe a purchase if a purchase is impossible.
3. Submit the notify form with a bad email and read the error.
4. Submit a valid one and read the confirmation.
5. Change variant, if variants exist, and watch the status follow.
6. Mark the item available and confirm the buy path is back, with the waitlist no longer pretending to be the hero.

If any step feels like a broken template, write the missing sentence before you add another recommendation row. The later sale depends on this page being believable while the shelf is empty.

Once the item can be bought, the next fact that same shopper needs is how it will arrive and what that costs. [Shipping copy on a product page](/blog/shipping-copy-on-a-product-page) is the piece to read next, because a true stock status still dies in the bag if the delivery window shows up as a surprise.

When this empty state is one of several screens the shop still has to design properly, [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) is how you and Hanabi can tell whether the work is a tighter product page or a fuller storefront.
